fields.h1: What Is Revival, and How Does It Begin?
fields.meta_title: What Is Revival, and How Does It Begin?
fields.description: Revival is God reviving his own people. Here is what revival actually is, what Scripture says about how it comes, and the lessons of one great awakening.
fields.body_html:
The word revival gets used loosely — a series of meetings, a burst of enthusiasm, a tent and a preacher. But biblical revival is something far deeper and less manageable: a sovereign visitation of God that breathes life back into his own people, until a lukewarm church becomes suddenly, unmistakably alive. It is not the same as evangelism, though many are converted in it. It is God reviving what is already his — and its effects can reshape whole nations.

What actually is revival, then, and how does it begin? Scripture has more to say than we often notice, and the history of one great awakening puts flesh on the answer.

Revival means God reviving his people

The heart of the word is life restored to something that had grown cold. The Psalmist’s cry is the classic prayer for it: “Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (Psalm 85:6). Notice who needs reviving — us, God’s people. Revival is not primarily about the world getting saved but about the church coming awake; the ingathering of outsiders follows a people set on fire.

Habakkuk prayed the same in a dark time: “O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years; in the midst of the years make it known; in wrath remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2). And Ezekiel was shown a valley of dry, scattered bones — a picture of a lifeless people — and watched the breath of God come into them until they stood, “an exceedingly great army” (Ezekiel 37:10). That is revival: God breathing on the dry bones of his own church until they live.

How Scripture says it comes

If revival is God’s sovereign act, is there nothing we can do but wait? Scripture holds a striking tension: revival is God’s gift, and yet it is repeatedly tied to what his people do. The most famous promise makes both plain: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Four things are asked of the people — humbling, praying, seeking, turning — and then God acts.

The pattern recurs. Hosea pleads, “Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the Lord, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you” (Hosea 10:12). Peter tells the crowd, “Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord” (Acts 3:19). The soil is prepared by humbling, repentance, and desperate prayer; the rain, when it comes, is God’s alone. And God has a particular address for it: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly” (Isaiah 57:15).

What revival is not

It clears the ground to say what revival is not, because much that borrows the name is something else. Revival is not mere excitement. Emotion often accompanies it — deep weeping, overflowing joy — but a stirred crowd is not the same as a visited church, and feelings that leave conduct unchanged are not revival at all. Nor is revival something we can schedule, engineer, or work up by the right techniques; that is to mistake the machinery for the wind, and “the wind blows where it wishes” (John 3:8). A revival that can be manufactured by human effort is exactly the kind of thing revival is not.

And revival is not chiefly about the spectacular. Its truest marks are unglamorous and moral: a sudden, piercing awareness of the holiness of God and the sinfulness of sin; confession and the making right of old wrongs; a hunger for Scripture and prayer; reconciliation between the estranged; and a joy that spills naturally into telling others. Where you see a church growing tender about sin, honest in confession, and glad in God, you are likely watching the real thing, whether or not anything dramatic ever makes the news. Where you see excitement without repentance, you are watching something else wearing revival’s clothes.

The lessons of one great awakening

The East African Revival, which began in the 1930s and swept through Rwanda, Uganda, and beyond for decades, is one of the clearest windows into how revival comes — and its story is written into Ochorus’s own library of African lives. It did not begin with a famous evangelist or a grand campaign. It began with two ordinary men and a hunger for more of God.

Simeon Nsibambi, a Ugandan believer, was gripped by a sense that the church — and his own heart — lacked the fullness and holiness of the New Testament. Blasio Kigozi, a young teacher and later deacon, was so burdened for a dead, formal Christianity that he withdrew to seek God, came back aflame, and pressed one urgent question on the church: Zukuka — “Awake!” He died of fever at barely thirty, but the awakening he pleaded for spread like fire. What marked it was not sensation but the very things Scripture names: deep conviction of sin, open confession and repentance, restored relationships, and a joy that overflowed into witness. Festo Kivengere, one of its later voices, became known across the world for a gospel of radical forgiveness forged in that fire.

Charles Finney, whose Lectures on Revivals of Religion shaped a century of thinking on the subject, insisted — sometimes too confidently — that revival follows when God’s people meet God’s conditions of humbling and prayer. Whatever the debates about his emphasis on human means, the East African story bears out the deeper truth underneath it: God pours out his Spirit on the lowly, the hungry, and the praying.

Prayer is the seedbed of every revival

If there is one thread running through every awakening in Scripture and history, it is prayer — not polished, occasional prayer, but desperate, persistent, corporate crying out to God. Before Pentecost, the disciples “with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer” (Acts 1:14), and then the Spirit fell. Nearly every revival since has been traced back, when its history is honestly written, to a handful of people who gave themselves to intercession long before anything visible happened — often praying for years in obscurity while the church around them slept.

This is enormously hopeful, because it means revival is not the preserve of the gifted or the platformed. It is available to any believer, any small group, any praying grandmother, willing to take God at his word and ask. Jesus made the staggering promise that the Father gives “the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11:13), and revival is, at bottom, the Spirit poured out. The East African Revival began with men who withdrew to seek God until they found him. The prayer that seeks revival is not a technique to force God’s hand; it is the God-given hunger through which he prepares to answer. If you long to see God move, the first place to look is not the platform but the prayer closet — and the first question is not “what program shall we run?” but “who among us will pray until he comes?”

How to seek it

So what do we do? Not manufacture revival — we cannot — but prepare the ground and cry out for the rain. That means honest repentance rather than vague wishing; it means broken, persistent prayer, personally and together; it means a hunger unwilling to settle for a comfortable, powerless Christianity. Joel’s promise still stands over every praying people: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

Every genuine revival in history has begun the same way — not with a program, but with a few people who became desperate for God and would not be content until he came. Revival is God’s to give. But he has never yet poured it out on a church that would not humble itself and pray, and he has never long withheld it from one that would.

Perhaps the most important thing to say is that revival begins in the singular before it spreads to the plural. Before God revives a church, he revives a heart — often one that simply grew tired of a Christianity with the form of godliness but little of its power, and began to seek him in earnest. You cannot schedule a national awakening. But you can ask God to revive you: to break up your own fallow ground, to make you tender about sin and hungry for him, to fill you afresh with his Spirit. That prayer he delights to answer, and history suggests he often begins the larger work through exactly such a beginning. Do not wait for the crowd. Let the reviving start where you are. Will you not revive us again?
